                    \delta=H-\Im s}}
 \frac{\delta M(s)}{N(k)(\delta/d_k)^{\beta_1}}.$$ The constants $L,c_0$ are chosen to cover the enlarged cones required by [thm:cone](#thm:cone), with exponent $1-\beta_1>1/2$, for a row point and its needed fixed neighborhoods.

<a id="critical:eq:cone-moments"></a>
Splitting the cone into unit ranges of logarithmic depth proves $$\label{critical:eq:cone-moments}
 \mathbb Eb(\cdot,k)\le C,
 \qquad
 \|b(\cdot,k)\|_p\le C_p(1+C_p^*)\quad(p\ge1),$$ whenever $\|d_jM\|_p\le C_p^*N(j)$ on all rows. Indeed, at a coarser level $j=k-h$, the normalized tile contribution is at most $C e^{-\beta_1h}N(j)/N(k)\le C e^{-(\beta_1-\beta)h}$ times its normalized row norm. These factors are summable. There are only a fixed number of finer levels because of $c_0$. The first inequality uses <a href="#critical:eq:first-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:first-moment">[critical:eq:first-moment]</a>; the second uses Minkowski’s inequality and <a href="#critical:eq:tile-averaging" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:tile-averaging">[critical:eq:tile-averaging]</a>.

<a id="stmt-critical-lem-one-sided"></a>
<div id="critical:lem:one-sided" class="lemma">

<a id="critical:eq:real-deficit"></a>
<a id="critical:eq:m-exponent"></a>
<a id="critical:eq:negative-P"></a>
**Lemma 48**. *Under <a href="#critical:eq:envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:envelope">[critical:eq:envelope]</a> and <a href="#critical:eq:first-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:first-moment">[critical:eq:first-moment]</a>, there are constants $c,z_0,C>0$ such that, for real $t$ and $z=|t|N(k)/d_k\le z_0$, $$\label{critical:eq:real-deficit}
 \Delta(t)\le C d_kz^\gamma,
 \qquad \gamma=\frac1{1+a}.$$ Moreover, with $$\label{critical:eq:m-exponent}
 m=\frac{4(2-\gamma)}{4-\gamma}<2,$$ one has $$\label{critical:eq:negative-P}
 \frac{d_kP^-(x+\mathrm i(H-d_k))}{N(k)^2}
 \le C b(x,k)^m.$$ Here $P^-$ is the nonnegative negative part of $P$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-critical-lem-one-sided"><summary>Proof of stmt-critical-lem-one-sided</summary>

<a id="critical:eq:Taylor-error"></a>
*Proof.* At a fixed center the cone theorem gives a joint holomorphic vertical passage at the row point for $$|t|<r_{x,k}:=c\frac{d_k}{N(k)b(x,k)}.$$ By decreasing $c$, and using a fixed slightly shallower target in the application of that theorem, it gives $|\mathfrak s-y|\le C d_k$ on this parameter disk and on a fixed neighborhood of the row point. The passage is attached to the actual lift from below and stays inside the shape strip. Evenness in $t$ and Cauchy’s estimate therefore give $$\label{critical:eq:Taylor-error}
 \left|\mathfrak s(y,t)-y-t^2V(y)\right|
 \le C d_k(zb(x,k))^4
 \quad\text{when }|t|\le r_{x,k}/2.$$ The fixed factors in $c$ are included in the constant here.

<a id="critical:eq:basic-width"></a>
By <a href="#critical:eq:cone-moments" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:cone-moments">[critical:eq:cone-moments]</a> there is a center with $b(x,k)\le C$. The real no-patch transfer from [thm:no-patch](#thm:no-patch) then implies $$\label{critical:eq:basic-width}
 \Delta(t)\le d_k
 \quad\text{for real }|t|\le c\,d_k/N(k).$$ This holds for all sufficiently large $k$; decreasing $c$ handles the remaining fixed compact range by joint analyticity near $t=0$.

For $j=k+h$, <a href="#critical:eq:envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:envelope">[critical:eq:envelope]</a> gives $$\frac{d_j}{N(j)}\ge C_N^{-1}
       \frac{d_k}{N(k)}e^{-(1+a)h}.$$ For small $z$, choose $h\ge0$ so that $e^{-h}=C'z^{1/(1+a)}$, where the fixed constant $C'$ is large enough for <a href="#critical:eq:basic-width" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:basic-width">[critical:eq:basic-width]</a> to apply at level $j$. This proves <a href="#critical:eq:real-deficit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:real-deficit">[critical:eq:real-deficit]</a>. Rounding $h$ to an integer, if desired, changes only a fixed constant.

For the negative part, take $z=c'b^{-4/(4-\gamma)}$, with $c'>0$ fixed sufficiently small. Since $b\ge1$, this makes both $zb$ and $\Delta(t)/d_k\le Cz^\gamma$ small. In particular the row lies strictly inside the actual strip. Its actual lift agrees with the vertical passage in <a href="#critical:eq:Taylor-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:Taylor-error">[critical:eq:Taylor-error]</a>. Combining that estimate with <a href="#critical:eq:lower-lift" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:lower-lift">[critical:eq:lower-lift]</a> gives $$\frac{d_kP^-}{N(k)^2}
 \le C\left(z^{\gamma-2}+z^2b^4\right).$$ The two powers of $b$ coincide and equal the exponent in <a href="#critical:eq:m-exponent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:m-exponent">[critical:eq:m-exponent]</a>. Since $\gamma>0$, that exponent is strictly less than two. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-69"></a>
#### The quadratic bootstrap and its moment improvement

<a id="stmt-critical-lem-disk-bound"></a>
<div id="critical:lem:disk-bound" class="lemma">

<a id="critical:eq:disk-bound"></a>
**Lemma 49**. *On an inner tile, with a fixed enlargement on the right, $$\label{critical:eq:disk-bound}
 (d_kM)^2\le C\left(1+\sup d_k^2|W|\right).$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-critical-lem-disk-bound"><summary>Proof of stmt-critical-lem-disk-bound</summary>

*Proof.* It is enough to prove the assertion on nested disks. In disk coordinates put $g=d_kf$ and $\widetilde W=d_k^2W$. Then $$g''=\frac18g(\widetilde W-g^2).$$ Suppose that no universal bound $\sup_{\mathbb D}|g|\le C(1+\sup_{2\mathbb D}|\widetilde W|)^{1/2}$ holds. For a counterexample sequence choose in an intermediate disk a point maximizing $|g(z)|$ times its distance to that disk’s boundary. Write $m_n$ for the value of $|g|$ there and $r_n$ for that distance. Failure of the proposed estimate implies $r_nm_n\to\infty$ and $\sup|\widetilde W|/m_n^2\to0$. On the disk of radius $r_n/2$ about the chosen point, maximality gives $|g|\le2m_n$. Rescale space by $m_n^{-1}$ and divide the function by $m_n$. After passage to a subsequence, the resulting functions converge on every compact subset of $\mathbb C$ to an entire function $G$ with $|G|\le2$, $|G(0)|=1$, and $G''=-G^3/8$. Liouville’s theorem makes $G$ constant, which contradicts this equation and $|G(0)|=1$. This bounds $f$. The identity $8q=W-f^2$ bounds $q$ on the same inner disk. A finite disk covering proves <a href="#critical:eq:disk-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:disk-bound">[critical:eq:disk-bound]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-thm-critical-bootstrap"></a>
<div id="thm:critical-bootstrap" class="theorem">

<a id="critical:eq:L2-bootstrap"></a>
<a id="critical:eq:higher-moment"></a>
<a id="critical:eq:global-envelope"></a>
**Theorem 50** (Critical moment bootstrap). *Let $N$ be an envelope as in [critical:def:envelope](#critical:def:envelope), assume the first-moment bound <a href="#critical:eq:first-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:first-moment">[critical:eq:first-moment]</a>, and suppose $\sup_{k\ge k_0}\mu(k)/N(k)<\infty$. Then $$\label{critical:eq:L2-bootstrap}
 \mu(k)\le C N(k),\qquad
 \mathbb E\frac{d_k|P|}{N(k)^2}\le C.$$ There is $\eta>0$, depending only on the fixed envelope constants, such that $$\label{critical:eq:higher-moment}
 \left\|\frac{d_kM}{N(k)}\right\|_{2+\eta}\le C.$$ The estimates for $M$ hold also with suprema on every fixed tile. If $N$ is nondecreasing, then in addition $$\label{critical:eq:global-envelope}
 \sup_x d_kM\le C(1+k)N(k),\qquad
 \sup_x\frac{d_k|P|}{N(k)^2}\le C(1+k)^2.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-thm-critical-bootstrap"><summary>Proof of stmt-thm-critical-bootstrap</summary>

*Proof of the quadratic and higher-moment assertions.* Let $C_* =\sup_{j\ge k_0}\mu(j)/N(j)<\infty$. By <a href="#critical:eq:cone-moments" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:cone-moments">[critical:eq:cone-moments]</a>, $\|b(\cdot,k)\|_2\le C(1+C_*)$. Hence <a href="#critical:eq:negative-P" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:negative-P">[critical:eq:negative-P]</a> gives $$\mathbb E\frac{d_kP^-}{N(k)^2}\le C(1+C_*^m).$$ The horizontal mean of $P$ is zero, so its positive and negative parts have equal integrals. Thus the same bound, with a factor two, holds for $|P|$.

Interior harmonic estimates bound the supremum of $|\nabla P|$ on a tile by $C d_k^{-3}$ times the integral of $|P|$ on a fixed enlargement. Averaging in the horizontal center and using the bounds on neighboring rows gives $$\mathbb E\sup_{\mathcal T_A(k,x)}
       \frac{d_k^2|W|}{N(k)^2}
 \le C_A(1+C_*^m).$$ Here <a href="#critical:eq:gradient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:gradient">[critical:eq:gradient]</a> accounts for the fixed additive constant $\langle W\rangle$, which is absorbed because $N\ge1$. The disk bound now yields $C_*^2\le C(1+C_*^m)$. Since $m<2$, this bounds $C_*$ by a fixed constant and proves <a href="#critical:eq:L2-bootstrap" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:L2-bootstrap">[critical:eq:L2-bootstrap]</a>, including the tile version of its first assertion.

<a id="critical:eq:negative-Lp"></a>
We give the concentration estimate that improves the moment. Put $p=2/m>1$ and $\vartheta=1-1/p>0$. The bound for $b$ and <a href="#critical:eq:negative-P" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:negative-P">[critical:eq:negative-P]</a> give, on all rows in any fixed range of depth ratios, $$\label{critical:eq:negative-Lp}
 \left\|\frac{d_kP^-}{N(k)^2}\right\|_p\le C.$$ Partition the horizontal circle into intervals of lengths comparable to $d_k$. Select a nonempty collection of fractional total length $\sigma$, and let $E$ be its enlargement by a fixed multiple of $d_k$. In particular $\sigma\ge c d_k$, and $|E|/(2\pi)\le C\sigma$. We estimate $P$ on $E$ on a row of depth $d'$ comparable to $d_k$.

<a id="critical:eq:strip-kernel"></a>
<a id="critical:eq:concentration-P"></a>
Choose $R\ge R_0$, with $R_0$ fixed sufficiently large, and suppose $Rd_k$ is small. Harmonic extension from that row to depth $Rd_k$, with zero data on the real row, is convolution with a positive periodic strip kernel $K$ of mass at most one. Before periodization its density is $$\label{critical:eq:strip-kernel}
 \frac1{2h'}
 \frac{\sin(\pi l/h')}
      {\cosh(\pi u/h')-\cos(\pi l/h')},
 \qquad h'=H-d',\quad l=Rd_k-d'.$$ It is at least $c/(Rd_k)$ when $|u|\le Rd_k$. Let $E_R$ be the enlargement of $E$ by a sufficiently large multiple of $Rd_k$; it has fractional length at most $C\min\{1,R\sigma\}$. Integrating first in the destination variable shows that a fixed fraction of the positive mass of $P$ on $E$ contributes to $\int_{E_R}K*P^+$. As $K*P^+=P_{\mathrm{coarse}}+K*P^-$, we obtain <a id="critical:eq:selected-P-plus"></a>$$\label{critical:eq:selected-P-plus}
 \int_E P^+\,\frac{\,\mathrm dx}{2\pi}
 \le C\left(\int |P_{\mathrm{coarse}}|\,\frac{\,\mathrm dx}{2\pi}
                  +\int_{E_R}K*P^-\,\frac{\,\mathrm dx}{2\pi}\right).$$ The normalized first term is at most $CR^{2\beta-1}$: at the coarse level $j=k-\log R$, use $N(j)\le C R^\beta N(k)$ and $d_j=Rd_k$ in <a href="#critical:eq:L2-bootstrap" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:L2-bootstrap">[critical:eq:L2-bootstrap]</a>. The convolution is an $L^p$ contraction, so Holder’s inequality and <a href="#critical:eq:negative-Lp" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:negative-Lp">[critical:eq:negative-Lp]</a> bound the second normalized term by $C(R\sigma)^\vartheta$. The negative mass directly on $E$ has the same bound. Consequently $$\label{critical:eq:concentration-P}
 \int_E\frac{d_k|P(x+\mathrm i(H-d'))|}{N(k)^2}
                \,\frac{\,\mathrm dx}{2\pi}
 \le C\left(R^{2\beta-1}+(R\sigma)^\vartheta\right).$$

<a id="critical:eq:concentration-M"></a>
The interior harmonic estimates used above, followed by [critical:lem:disk-bound](#critical:lem:disk-bound), now give $$\label{critical:eq:concentration-M}
 \sum_{I\ \mathrm{selected}} |I|
       \sup_{x\in I}\sup_{s\in\mathcal T_A(k,x)}
                  \frac{d_k^2M(s)^2}{N(k)^2}
 \le C_A\left(\sigma+R^{2\beta-1}+(R\sigma)^\vartheta\right).$$ To see that no concentration is lost in this passage, enlarge the selected intervals by the fixed horizontal margins needed for the harmonic estimates and integrate those estimates over the fixed range of neighboring depths. The enlarged intervals have bounded overlap and still total length $O(\sigma)$, so <a href="#critical:eq:concentration-P" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:concentration-P">[critical:eq:concentration-P]</a> applies at every such depth.

Take $R=R_0\sigma^{-1/2}$. This is allowed for all sufficiently large $k$, since $\sigma\ge c d_k$ gives $Rd_k\le C\sqrt{d_k}$. The remaining compact range of $k$ is harmless. There is therefore $0<\zeta<1$, depending only on $\beta$ and $p$, such that the right side of <a href="#critical:eq:concentration-M" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:concentration-M">[critical:eq:concentration-M]</a> is at most $C_A\sigma^\zeta$. For example one may take any positive $\zeta$ no larger than $\min\{(1-2\beta)/2,\vartheta/2\}$.

Let $A_k(I)$ be the supremum appearing in the sum in <a href="#critical:eq:concentration-M" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:concentration-M">[critical:eq:concentration-M]</a>. Selecting the cells for which $A_k(I)>b_0\ge1$ gives $$\mathbb P\{A_k>b_0\}\le C b_0^{-1/(1-\zeta)}.$$ The exponent is greater than one. Integrating this distribution bound shows that $A_k$ has a uniformly bounded moment of some order $1+\eta/2>1$. This proves <a href="#critical:eq:higher-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:higher-moment">[critical:eq:higher-moment]</a>, including its fixed-tile versions. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-thm-critical-bootstrap-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-thm-critical-bootstrap</summary>

<a id="critical:eq:complex-deficit"></a>
<a id="critical:eq:diameter-integral"></a>
*Proof of the global assertions in [thm:critical-bootstrap](#thm:critical-bootstrap).* Suppose $N$ is nondecreasing. We first prove that, for a fixed small $c_2>0$, $$\label{critical:eq:complex-deficit}
 \Delta(t)\le d_k/4\qquad
 \left(|t|\le \rho_k:=\frac{c_2d_k}{(1+k)N(k)}\right).$$ Choose a fixed $\varepsilon_0>0$ so small that <a href="#critical:eq:real-deficit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:real-deficit">[critical:eq:real-deficit]</a> bounds $\Delta$ by $d_k/16$ on the real interval $|u|\le u_0:=\varepsilon_0d_k/N(k)$. For a fixed small parameter half-disk, harmonic upper comparison for the bounded subharmonic function $\Delta$ gives, when $|t|\le u_0/2$, an upper bound consisting of this near-diameter contribution, an $O(|t|)$ contribution from the curved boundary, and $$\label{critical:eq:diameter-integral}
 C|t|\int_{u_0}^{r_0}
         \max\{\Delta(u),\Delta(-u)\}\,\frac{\,\mathrm du}{u^2}.$$ Here $r_0>0$ is fixed. The kernel bound follows directly from the upper-half-plane Poisson kernel on the diameter; the harmonic measure of the distant curved arc is $O(|t|)$. Upper semicontinuous boundary data cause no difficulty: apply the comparison first to continuous majorants and decrease them to the given data. The lower half-disk is handled in the same way.

We claim that the integral in <a href="#critical:eq:diameter-integral" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:diameter-integral">[critical:eq:diameter-integral]</a> is at most $C_{\varepsilon_0}(1+k)N(k)$. For earlier levels $j\le k$, monotonicity gives $N(j)\le N(k)$, so <a href="#critical:eq:basic-width" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:basic-width">[critical:eq:basic-width]</a> implies $\Delta(u)\le d_j$ up to $|u|\le c d_j/N(k)$. Divide the interval of integration into the corresponding ranges for $j=k,k-1,\ldots$, down to a fixed level. On each such range $\Delta(u)\le C d_j$ and its $u^{-2}$ integral is at most $C N(k)$. The first range costs $C_{\varepsilon_0}N(k)$. Beyond the last one the boundedness of $\Delta$ costs at most $C N(k)$. There are $O(1+k)$ ranges, proving the claim. Choosing $c_2$ small now proves <a href="#critical:eq:complex-deficit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:complex-deficit">[critical:eq:complex-deficit]</a>.

For $y$ at depth comparable to $d_k$, with a fixed neighborhood of that size, the actual lift is consequently holomorphic for $|t|<\rho_k$ and satisfies $\Im(\mathfrak s(y,t)-y)\le C d_k$. It vanishes at $t=0$. The coefficient estimate for an analytic function with positive real part, applied to $C d_k+\mathrm i(\mathfrak s-y)$, gives $$|V(y)|\le C d_k\rho_k^{-2}.$$ This elementary estimate also follows by integrating the nonnegative real part on concentric circles and taking its second Fourier coefficient. It proves the asserted bound for $P$. Cauchy’s estimate in $y$, followed by <a href="#critical:eq:gradient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:gradient">[critical:eq:gradient]</a>, gives $|W|\le C\rho_k^{-2}+C$ on a slightly smaller tile. The disk bound therefore gives $d_kM\le C d_k/\rho_k+C$, which is the other assertion in <a href="#critical:eq:global-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:global-envelope">[critical:eq:global-envelope]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-70"></a>
#### A weighted version with an ancestor row

<a id="critical:eq:ancestor-kernel"></a>
We will need to concentrate horizontal centers near a selected ancestor, while retaining estimates at much finer depths. For $0<d_a\ll1$, let $K_{d_a}$ be a normalized periodic probability kernel whose density, relative to $\,\mathrm dx/(2\pi)$, is uniformly comparable to $$\label{critical:eq:ancestor-kernel}
 \frac{d_a}{d_a^2+|x|_{\mathrm{per}}^2}.$$ The normalization factor in this comparison is bounded above and below independently of $d_a$. Given any probability $\omega$ on the circle, put $\nu=K_{d_a}*\omega$. The following elementary properties will be used.

First, for every fixed $A$, the density of $\nu$ changes by at most a fixed factor under translations of length at most $A d_a$. For the kernel this follows from the triangle inequality and $$d_a^2+|u+h|_{\mathrm{per}}^2
 \le C_A(d_a^2+|u|_{\mathrm{per}}^2)
 \quad (|h|\le A d_a),$$ and convolution preserves the comparison. Second, if $d_j<d_a/2$, the unnormalized upper-boundary harmonic-measure law from the ancestor point $x+\mathrm i(H-d_a)$ to the row at depth $d_j$, with real bottom, is uniformly comparable to the translated kernel $K_{d_a}$. Indeed in <a href="#critical:eq:strip-kernel" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:strip-kernel">[critical:eq:strip-kernel]</a> the distance from the upper row lies between $d_a/2$ and $d_a$. On a fundamental horizontal interval the denominator is comparable to $d_a^2+|u|^2$, with constants depending only on $H$; periodization contributes a comparable bounded tail. Mixing over $\omega$ gives an unnormalized law comparable to $\nu$.

<a id="stmt-prop-weighted-bootstrap"></a>
<div id="prop:weighted-bootstrap" class="proposition">

<a id="critical:eq:weighted-coarse"></a>
<a id="critical:eq:weighted-conclusion"></a>
**Proposition 51**. *Let $N$ satisfy the hypotheses of [thm:critical-bootstrap](#thm:critical-bootstrap), with fixed constants, and let $d_a=e^{-k_a}$ be a sufficiently small ancestor depth. Let $\omega,\nu$ be as above, with fixed kernel comparison constants. Suppose that for every fixed tile enlargement needed below, $$\label{critical:eq:weighted-coarse}
 \left\|\sup_{s\in\mathcal T_A(j,x)}d_jM(s)\right\|_{L^2(\nu)}
 \le C_A N(j),\qquad k_0\le j\le k_a+3,$$ and that <a id="critical:eq:weighted-anchor"></a>$$\label{critical:eq:weighted-anchor}
 \int |P(x+\mathrm i(H-d_a))|\,\,\mathrm d\omega(x)
 \le C\frac{N(k_a)^2}{d_a}.$$ Then on all finer levels, and with every fixed tile enlargement, $$\label{critical:eq:weighted-conclusion}
 \left\|\sup_{s\in\mathcal T_A(j,x)}d_jM(s)\right\|_{L^2(\nu)}
 \le C'_A N(j).$$ The constants are independent of $k_a$, of $\omega$, and of the finite bootstrap ratio. No higher weighted moment is asserted.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-weighted-bootstrap"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-weighted-bootstrap</summary>

*Proof.* It suffices first to bound row norms. Let $C_*$ be their supremum ratio to $N$ on the fine levels, enlarged to include the fixed coarse constants. This number is finite. For example, the density of $\nu$ is bounded for each fixed ancestor, so finiteness follows from the unweighted finite-ratio hypothesis. This preliminary bound may depend on $d_a$; none of the estimates below will depend on it.

<a id="critical:eq:weighted-b"></a>
Tile averaging on levels whose depths are at most a fixed multiple of $d_a$ is valid for $\nu$, by its translation-comparison property. In the logarithmic summation defining $b$, use these fine tile bounds on that part of the cone, and use <a href="#critical:eq:weighted-coarse" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:weighted-coarse">[critical:eq:weighted-coarse]</a> on the coarser part. This gives $$\label{critical:eq:weighted-b}
 \|b(\cdot,j)\|_{L^2(\nu)}\le C(1+C_*).$$ Fixed ranges immediately adjacent to the coarse cutoff are already covered by the assumed fixed tile enlargements at levels at most $k_a+3$. In particular, choosing larger fixed interior-estimate neighborhoods does not create a gap at the cutoff.

<a id="critical:eq:anchor-decay"></a>
For $d_j<d_a/2$, let $\kappa_j$ be the mixed unnormalized harmonic-measure law from $\omega$ to the row at depth $d_j$. Since $P=0$ on the real bottom, $$\int P(x+\mathrm i(H-d_j))\,\,\mathrm d\kappa_j(x)
   =\int P(x+\mathrm i(H-d_a))\,\,\mathrm d\omega(x).$$ The laws $\kappa_j$ and $\nu$ are comparable. Moreover the absolute value of the right side, in fine-row normalization, is at most $$\label{critical:eq:anchor-decay}
 C\frac{d_j}{d_a}\frac{N(k_a)^2}{N(j)^2}
 \le C e^{-(1-2\beta)(j-k_a)}\le C.$$ The negative-part estimate <a href="#critical:eq:negative-P" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:negative-P">[critical:eq:negative-P]</a>, integrated using <a href="#critical:eq:weighted-b" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:weighted-b">[critical:eq:weighted-b]</a>, bounds the normalized negative integral by $C(1+C_*^m)$. Taking the signed integral under $\kappa_j$ first, and then using comparison of the two positive measures, therefore gives $$\int\frac{d_j|P(x+\mathrm i(H-d_j))|}{N(j)^2}\,\,\mathrm d\nu(x)
 \le C(1+C_*^m).$$ The strict inequality $2\beta<1$ gives uniform decay in <a href="#critical:eq:anchor-decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:anchor-decay">[critical:eq:anchor-decay]</a>.

Weighted interior harmonic estimates now follow by the same local averaging argument, since the required horizontal translations are of size $O(d_j)$. Combining them with [critical:lem:disk-bound](#critical:lem:disk-bound) gives $C_*^2\le C(1+C_*^m)$, away from the already controlled fixed cutoff range. This bounds $C_*$ uniformly. One more application of weighted tile averaging proves <a href="#critical:eq:weighted-conclusion" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:weighted-conclusion">[critical:eq:weighted-conclusion]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-71"></a>
#### A vanishing profile at one center is impossible

The next result is deliberately stated for individual centers. A single quiet cone forces a global real-parameter width estimate, and the latter can then be tested against unweighted horizontal moments.

<a id="stmt-thm-no-trivial-profile"></a>
<div id="thm:no-trivial-profile" class="theorem">

**Theorem 52** (Exclusion of vanishing profiles at individual centers). *Consider sequences of levels $k_n\to\infty$, scales $d_n=e^{-k_n}$, and amplitudes $B_n=\mu(k_n)\to\infty$. Suppose there are envelopes $N_n$ satisfying the hypotheses of [thm:critical-bootstrap](#thm:critical-bootstrap) with constants independent of $n$, and $N_n(k_n)\le C B_n$.*

<a id="critical:eq:quiet-cone"></a>
<a id="critical:eq:profiles"></a>
<a id="critical:eq:bounded-coarse-cone"></a>
*For a fixed $\alpha\in(1/2,1)$ and a sufficiently large fixed aperture $L$, there cannot be centers $x_n$ such that, for every fixed $c>0$, $$\label{critical:eq:quiet-cone}
 \sup_{\substack{c d_n\le\delta\le\delta_b\\
                  |\Re s-x_n|\le L\delta\\
                  \delta=H-\Im s}}
 \frac{d_nM(s)}{B_n}\left(\frac{\delta}{d_n}\right)^\alpha
 \longrightarrow0.$$ In particular, suppose the profiles $$\label{critical:eq:profiles}
 F_n(S)=\frac{d_n}{B_n}f(x_n+\mathrm iH+d_nS),\qquad
 Q_n(S)=\left(\frac{d_n}{B_n}\right)^2q(x_n+\mathrm iH+d_nS)$$ converge to $(0,0)$ on compact subsets of the lower half-plane. They cannot also satisfy, for some fixed $\alpha_0>1/2$ and an aperture $L$ sufficiently large for a chosen exponent $1/2<\alpha<\min(1,\alpha_0)$, $$\label{critical:eq:bounded-coarse-cone}
 \frac{d_n}{B_n}M(s)\le C\left(\frac{d_n}{\delta}\right)^{\alpha_0}
 \quad(d_n\le\delta\le\delta_b,
             \ |\Re s-x_n|\le L\delta).$$ Every compact holomorphic limit of the pair in <a href="#critical:eq:profiles" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:profiles">[critical:eq:profiles]</a> is pure: its product $FQ$ vanishes identically.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-thm-no-trivial-profile"><summary>Proof of stmt-thm-no-trivial-profile</summary>

<a id="critical:eq:vanishing-width"></a>
*Proof.* Suppose first that <a href="#critical:eq:quiet-cone" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:quiet-cone">[critical:eq:quiet-cone]</a> holds. For any fixed $c,T_0>0$, apply [thm:cone](#thm:cone) at a depth which is a fixed small multiple of $c d_n$, and with parameter radius $T_0d_n/B_n$. The ratio of this radius to the target depth tends to zero. Thus its fixed $K=1$ regime suffices, and its aperture can be chosen once, independently of $c,T_0$. The weighted smallness in <a href="#critical:eq:quiet-cone" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:quiet-cone">[critical:eq:quiet-cone]</a> supplies its small parameter. The real no-patch transfer gives $$\Delta(Td_n/B_n)\le c d_n
 \quad (|T|\le T_0)$$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Since $c>0$ is arbitrary, $$\label{critical:eq:vanishing-width}
 \sup_{|T|\le T_0}\frac{\Delta(Td_n/B_n)}{d_n}\longrightarrow0
 \qquad(T\text{ real}).$$

<a id="critical:eq:uniform-integrability"></a>
We show that this width estimate alone contradicts $B_n=\mu(k_n)$. Let $j-k_n$ vary in an arbitrary fixed compact interval. The envelope inequalities imply $N_n(j)\le C B_n$, with a constant uniform on that interval. By the quadratic bootstrap and <a href="#critical:eq:cone-moments" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:cone-moments">[critical:eq:cone-moments]</a>, the cone costs $b(x,j)$ have uniformly bounded second moments. Also <a href="#critical:eq:negative-P" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:negative-P">[critical:eq:negative-P]</a> gives $$\label{critical:eq:uniform-integrability}
 \frac{d_nP^-(x+\mathrm i(H-d_j))}{B_n^2}\le C b(x,j)^m,
 \qquad m<2.$$ These variables are uniformly integrable: their $2/m$-moments are bounded, and $2/m>1$.

Fix a cutoff $A>1$ and work where $b(x,j)\le A$. Take $t=T d_n/B_n$ with a fixed nonzero $T$ small enough for the Taylor estimate at all these points. By <a href="#critical:eq:vanishing-width" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:vanishing-width">[critical:eq:vanishing-width]</a>, the relevant rows lie in the actual strip for large $n$. Combining <a href="#critical:eq:lower-lift" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:lower-lift">[critical:eq:lower-lift]</a> and <a href="#critical:eq:Taylor-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:Taylor-error">[critical:eq:Taylor-error]</a>, now in this normalization, gives $$\frac{d_nP^-}{B_n^2}
 \le C\frac{\Delta(Td_n/B_n)}{T^2d_n}+C T^2 A^4.$$ Given a positive threshold, first choose $A$ so that the complement has small probability, then choose $|T|$ so that the second term is below that threshold, and finally let $n\to\infty$. This proves convergence to zero in probability. The uniform integrability in <a href="#critical:eq:uniform-integrability" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:uniform-integrability">[critical:eq:uniform-integrability]</a> gives convergence in mean, uniformly on every fixed range of $j-k_n$.

The signed horizontal mean of $P$ is zero, so the same conclusion holds for $d_n|P|/B_n^2$. Interior harmonic estimates, using a fixed range of neighboring depths, imply $$\mathbb E\sup_{\text{fixed tile}}
       \frac{d_n^2|W|}{B_n^2}\longrightarrow0.$$ The disk bound and $B_n\to\infty$ now imply $$\frac{\mu(k_n)^2}{B_n^2}\longrightarrow0,$$ contradicting its value one.

For the stated consequence, choose $1/2<\alpha<\min\{1,\alpha_0\}$. On the part of the cone with $\delta/d_n\ge R$, <a href="#critical:eq:bounded-coarse-cone" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:bounded-coarse-cone">[critical:eq:bounded-coarse-cone]</a> bounds the expression in <a href="#critical:eq:quiet-cone" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:quiet-cone">[critical:eq:quiet-cone]</a> by $C R^{\alpha-\alpha_0}$. On each remaining compact part with $c\le\delta/d_n\le R$, the assumed profile convergence makes it tend to zero. Letting $R\to\infty$ proves <a href="#critical:eq:quiet-cone" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:quiet-cone">[critical:eq:quiet-cone]</a>, which was just excluded. In fact compact convergence within this fixed cone is enough for the argument.

Finally the scaled differential identity is $$\partial_S^2F_n=B_n^2Q_nF_n.$$ Compact holomorphic convergence bounds its left side. Dividing by $B_n^2$ and passing to the limit gives $FQ=0$. On the connected lower half-plane, a nonzero analytic factor then forces the other factor to vanish identically. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-72"></a>
#### The sequence to be excluded and the angle-budget reduction

We specify the input to the next Section before deriving the consequences of its exclusion. For a probability $\nu_n$ on horizontal centers, convergence in probability uniformly on a compact set means that the probability of the supremum exceeding each fixed positive threshold tends to zero.

<a id="stmt-def-prohibited-sequence"></a>
<div id="def:prohibited-sequence" class="definition">

**Definition 53**. A prohibited sequence consists of the following data in the critical setting of this Section:

1.  Levels $k_n\to\infty$, amplitudes $B_n=\mu(k_n)\to\infty$, and numbers $\varepsilon_n\downarrow0$ such that <a id="critical:eq:primary-normality"></a>$$\label{critical:eq:primary-normality}
      \mu(j)\le B_n e^{\varepsilon_n|j-k_n|}
           \qquad(j\ge k_0).$$

2.  Ancestors $k_{a,n}=k_n-s_n$, with both $k_{a,n}\to\infty$ and $s_n\to\infty$, and probabilities $\omega_n$ and $\nu_n=K_{d_{a,n}}*\omega_n$, where $d_{a,n}=e^{-k_{a,n}}$ and the kernels obey <a href="#critical:eq:ancestor-kernel" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:ancestor-kernel">[critical:eq:ancestor-kernel]</a> with comparison constants independent of $n$.

<a id="critical:eq:prohibited-coarse"></a>
<a id="critical:eq:prohibited-anchor"></a>
3.  For every fixed $0<\beta<1/2$ and every fixed tile enlargement $A$, there is a constant $C_{\beta,A}$ such that, eventually in $n$, simultaneously for all $k_0\le j\le k_{a,n}+3$, $$\label{critical:eq:prohibited-coarse}
      \left\|\sup_{s\in\mathcal T_A(j,x)}d_jM(s)\right\|_{L^2(\nu_n)}
       \le C_{\beta,A} B_n e^{\beta(k_n-j)}.$$ For every such $\beta$ there is also a constant $C_\beta$ such that, eventually, $$\label{critical:eq:prohibited-anchor}
      \int |P(x+\mathrm i(H-d_{a,n}))|\,\,\mathrm d\omega_n(x)
       \le C_\beta
           \frac{B_n^2e^{2\beta(k_n-k_{a,n})}}{d_{a,n}}.$$ The constants and the threshold for “eventually” may depend on the indicated fixed choices, but not on $j$ or $n$.

<a id="critical:eq:prohibited-Q"></a>
4.  With $d_n=e^{-k_n}$, for every compact subset $\mathcal K$ of $\{\Im S<0\}$, $$\label{critical:eq:prohibited-Q}
      \sup_{S\in\mathcal K}
      \left|\left(\frac{d_n}{B_n}\right)^2
              q(x+\mathrm iH+d_nS)\right|
      \longrightarrow0
      \quad\text{in }\nu_n\text{-probability}.$$

</div>

For fixed $\beta,a>0$, with $\beta<1/2$, primary normality controls the unweighted moments by an envelope of the form $$N_n(j)=B_n
   \exp\bigl(\beta(k_n-j)_++a(j-k_n)_+\bigr).$$ Thus [prop:weighted-bootstrap](#prop:weighted-bootstrap) applies to this envelope using <a href="#critical:eq:prohibited-coarse" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:prohibited-coarse">[critical:eq:prohibited-coarse]</a> and <a href="#critical:eq:prohibited-anchor" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:prohibited-anchor">[critical:eq:prohibited-anchor]</a>. This observation uses none of the conditional conclusions below. It is the reason the ancestors are included in the definition.

<a id="critical:eq:deficit-step"></a>
We will also use an elementary way to propagate a logarithmic deficit. If $U\ge0$ is superharmonic and two small disks have comparable radii, nearby centers, and a sufficiently enlarged common disk contained in its domain, then $$\label{critical:eq:deficit-step}
 \operatorname{av}_{D_2}U\le C\operatorname{av}_{D_1}U.$$ Indeed, for each point of $D_1$, a disk centered there and of a fixed multiple of the common radius contains $D_2$ and remains inside the domain. Positivity and the supermean inequality bound the average on $D_2$ by a constant times the value at that point; integration over $D_1$ proves the claim. Starting with a disk centered at a point where $U$ is finite, the first average is at most that value. A chain of $m$ such steps therefore costs at most $C^m$. In the upper strip, one can connect points with logarithmic depth separation $s$, and with a horizontal displacement bounded by a fixed multiple of the larger depth, by $O(1+s)$ disks of radii small fixed multiples of their depths. All enlarged disks can be kept in a fixed slightly wider range of logarithmic depths. This argument applies to $K-\log|f|$, including its logarithmic poles at zeros; it uses disk averages, not a pointwise Harnack inequality for superharmonic functions.

<a id="stmt-critical-prop-power-saving"></a>
<div id="critical:prop:power-saving" class="proposition">

<a id="critical:eq:mu-f-saving"></a>
**Proposition 54**. *Assume that no sequence in [def:prohibited-sequence](#def:prohibited-sequence) exists. Then there are $C>0$ and $\varepsilon_1\in(0,1)$ such that $$\label{critical:eq:mu-f-saving}
 \mu_f(k)\le C(1+k)^{1-\varepsilon_1}\qquad(k\ge k_0).$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-critical-prop-power-saving"><summary>Proof of stmt-critical-prop-power-saving</summary>

<a id="critical:eq:f-record"></a>
*Proof.* Suppose otherwise. We first choose levels $\kappa_n\to\infty$ and values $b_n=\mu_f(\kappa_n)$ such that $$\label{critical:eq:f-record}
 \begin{split}
 b_n&\ge\kappa_n^{1-o(1)},\\
 \mu_f(j)&\le b_n\quad(k_0\le j\le\kappa_n),\\
 \mu_f(j)&\le b_n e^{\eta_n(j-\kappa_n)}
       \quad(j\ge\kappa_n),\qquad \eta_n\to0.
 \end{split}$$ Here is an explicit selection. Failure of <a href="#critical:eq:mu-f-saving" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:mu-f-saving">[critical:eq:mu-f-saving]</a> provides arbitrarily large levels with $\mu_f\ge k^{1-1/n}$. Replace such a level by a maximum of $\mu_f$ over all earlier levels; denote the resulting record level by $u_n$. The record values tend to infinity, so $u_n\to\infty$, and they still exceed $u_n^{1-1/n}$. Choose $\eta_n\to0$ with $\eta_n\ge1/u_n$. Maximize $\mu_f(j)e^{-\eta_n(j-u_n)}$ on $j\ge u_n$, and call a maximizer $\kappa_n$. It exists by <a href="#critical:eq:subexponential" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:subexponential">[critical:eq:subexponential]</a>. It is still a record among all earlier levels. Its value satisfies $$b_n\ge u_n^{1-1/n}e^{\eta_n(\kappa_n-u_n)}
       \ge\kappa_n^{1-1/n},$$ where we used $\log(\kappa_n/u_n)\le(\kappa_n-u_n)/u_n$. The maximizing property gives the last inequality in <a href="#critical:eq:f-record" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:f-record">[critical:eq:f-record]</a>.

<a id="critical:eq:record-envelope"></a>
<a id="critical:eq:event-cost"></a>
For each fixed $\eta>0$, and all sufficiently large $n$, set $$N_{n,\eta}(j)=(b_n+\kappa_n)
                   e^{\eta(j-\kappa_n)_+}.$$ This nondecreasing envelope controls the first moment uniformly in $n$. For $|f|$ use <a href="#critical:eq:f-record" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:f-record">[critical:eq:f-record]</a>; for $|q|^{1/2}$ use <a href="#critical:eq:q-first-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:q-first-moment">[critical:eq:q-first-moment]</a> and $1+j\le C_\eta(1+\kappa_n)e^{\eta(j-\kappa_n)}$ on the future side. Its finite-ratio hypothesis follows from its exponential tail. [thm:critical-bootstrap](#thm:critical-bootstrap) consequently gives $$\label{critical:eq:record-envelope}
 \mu(j)\le C_\eta(b_n+\kappa_n)e^{\eta(j-\kappa_n)_+},\qquad
 d_j\max M\le C_\eta(1+j)(b_n+\kappa_n)
                         e^{\eta(j-\kappa_n)_+}.$$ Fix one positive $\eta$ to use the higher-moment assertion, and let $p>2$ be the resulting exponent. On the row $\kappa_n$ put $$E_n=\{x:d_{\kappa_n}|f(x+\mathrm i(H-d_{\kappa_n}))|\ge b_n/2\},
 \qquad p_n=\mathbb P(E_n).$$ Holder’s inequality gives $$\frac34 b_n^2
 \le C(b_n+\kappa_n)^2p_n^{1-2/p}.$$ Therefore $$\label{critical:eq:event-cost}
 p_n\ge c\left(\frac{b_n}{b_n+\kappa_n}\right)^{2p/(p-2)}
       =\kappa_n^{-o(1)}.$$

<a id="critical:eq:discount-normality"></a>
<a id="critical:eq:small-shift"></a>
We next select a normal level for the full moment. For any fixed small $\varepsilon>0$, maximize $\mu(j)e^{-\varepsilon|j-\kappa_n|}$ over $j\ge k_0$. Let $k$ be a maximizer and $B=\mu(k)$. The triangle inequality gives $$\label{critical:eq:discount-normality}
 \mu(j)\le B e^{\varepsilon|j-k|},\qquad B\ge b_n.$$ Using <a href="#critical:eq:record-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:record-envelope">[critical:eq:record-envelope]</a> with rate $\varepsilon/2$ also gives $$|k-\kappa_n|\le\frac2\varepsilon
         \log\left(\frac{C_\varepsilon(b_n+\kappa_n)}{b_n}\right).$$ For fixed $\varepsilon$, the right side is $o(\log\kappa_n)$, by <a href="#critical:eq:f-record" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:f-record">[critical:eq:f-record]</a>. A slow diagonal choice thus gives $\varepsilon_n\downarrow0$ and maximizing levels $k_n$ such that $$\label{critical:eq:small-shift}
 B_n^{\mathrm{new}}:=\mu(k_n)\ge b_n,
 \qquad |k_n-\kappa_n|=o(\log\kappa_n),$$ while <a href="#critical:eq:discount-normality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:discount-normality">[critical:eq:discount-normality]</a> holds with $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_n$. For the remainder of this proof write $B_n=B_n^{\mathrm{new}}$; the record value remains denoted by $b_n$.

Choose $s_n\to\infty$, $s_n=o(\log\kappa_n)$, so slowly that it dominates both $|k_n-\kappa_n|$ and $\log(1/p_n)$. Such a choice is possible by <a href="#critical:eq:event-cost" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:event-cost">[critical:eq:event-cost]</a> and <a href="#critical:eq:small-shift" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:small-shift">[critical:eq:small-shift]</a>; for example take the geometric mean of $\log\kappa_n$ and $1+|k_n-\kappa_n|+\log(1/p_n)$. Set $k_{a,n}=k_n-s_n$, let $\omega_n$ be uniform horizontal measure conditioned on $E_n$, and let $\nu_n=K_{d_{a,n}}*\omega_n$. Both $\omega_n$ and $\nu_n$ have densities at most $p_n^{-1}=e^{o(s_n)}$ relative to uniform measure.

We check all ancestor bounds. Fix $0<\beta<1/2$, a tile enlargement, and $0<\beta_0<\beta$. Primary normality and tile averaging give the unweighted bound $$\left\|\sup_{\mathcal T_A(j,x)}d_jM\right\|_2
 \le C_A B_n e^{\beta_0(k_n-j)}
 \quad(j\le k_{a,n}+3)$$ for large $n$. Passing to $\nu_n$ costs at most $p_n^{-1/2}$. This is absorbed by $e^{(\beta-\beta_0)(k_n-j)}$, uniformly on that range because $k_n-j\ge s_n-3$. For the anchor, apply the $P$ estimate of [thm:critical-bootstrap](#thm:critical-bootstrap) to the envelope $$B_n\exp\bigl(\beta_0(k_n-j)_++a_0(j-k_n)_+\bigr)$$ with any fixed $a_0>0$. Primary normality supplies its hypotheses. Conditioning costs $p_n^{-1}$, which is absorbed by $e^{2(\beta-\beta_0)s_n}$. This proves <a href="#critical:eq:prohibited-coarse" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:prohibited-coarse">[critical:eq:prohibited-coarse]</a> and <a href="#critical:eq:prohibited-anchor" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:prohibited-anchor">[critical:eq:prohibited-anchor]</a>, with constants independent of $n$ for every fixed choice.

It remains to prove <a href="#critical:eq:prohibited-Q" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:prohibited-Q">[critical:eq:prohibited-Q]</a>. Fix a compact set $\mathcal K$ in the lower half-plane and a fixed $A>1$. For a center $x_0\in E_n$, consider all target disks needed to control $q$ on $x+\mathrm iH+d_n\mathcal K$, where $|x-x_0|_{\mathrm{per}}\le A d_{a,n}$. One can connect the initial point at level $\kappa_n$ to these disks by first moving to the ancestor row, moving horizontally there, and then moving to the target depth. The number of depth-sized disks required is $O_A(1+s_n+|k_n-\kappa_n|)=o(\log\kappa_n)$.

On a fixed enlargement of this entire range, <a href="#critical:eq:record-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:record-envelope">[critical:eq:record-envelope]</a> implies $$\log|f|\le U_n^*:=\kappa_n+\log b_n+C\log\kappa_n.$$ Here $C$ can be fixed: all level changes are $o(\log\kappa_n)$, and $\log((b_n+\kappa_n)/b_n)=o(\log\kappa_n)$. At the initial point in $E_n$, the nonnegative superharmonic deficit $U_n^*-\log|f|$ is $O(\log\kappa_n)$. The disk-chain estimate <a href="#critical:eq:deficit-step" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:deficit-step">[critical:eq:deficit-step]</a> bounds its average on every target disk by $\kappa_n^{o(1)}$, uniformly in the indicated centers. [lem:log-deficit](#lem:log-deficit), with fixed inner margins, therefore gives $$\sup_{S\in\mathcal K}d_n
       |q(x+\mathrm iH+d_nS)|^{1/2}\le\kappa_n^{o(1)}.$$ Since $B_n\ge b_n\ge\kappa_n^{1-o(1)}$, this is negligible relative to $B_n$.

Under $\nu_n$, a center can be sampled by first choosing $x_0$ with law $\omega_n$ and then adding the kernel increment. The probability that its periodic distance exceeds $A d_{a,n}$ is at most $C/A$, uniformly in $n$. For every fixed $A$, the preceding estimate holds on the complement. First let $n\to\infty$, and then let $A\to\infty$. This proves <a href="#critical:eq:prohibited-Q" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:prohibited-Q">[critical:eq:prohibited-Q]</a>. We have constructed all the data of [def:prohibited-sequence](#def:prohibited-sequence), a contradiction. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-cor-critical-polynomial-bounds"></a>
<div id="cor:critical-polynomial-bounds" class="corollary">

<a id="critical:eq:polynomial-bounds"></a>
**Corollary 55**. *Assume that no sequence in [def:prohibited-sequence](#def:prohibited-sequence) exists. Then, for all $k\ge k_0$, $$\label{critical:eq:polynomial-bounds}
 \mu(k)\le C(1+k),\qquad
 d_k\max_x M\le C(1+k)^2,\qquad
 d_k\max_x|P|\le C(1+k)^4.$$ All fixed tile enlargements have the corresponding bounds.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-cor-critical-polynomial-bounds"><summary>Proof of stmt-cor-critical-polynomial-bounds</summary>

*Proof.* By [critical:prop:power-saving](#critical:prop:power-saving) and <a href="#critical:eq:q-first-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:q-first-moment">[critical:eq:q-first-moment]</a>, $\mathbb Ed_jM\le C(1+j)$. At a target level $K$, use the nondecreasing envelope $$N_K(j)=
 \begin{cases}
  1+j,&k_0\le j\le K,\\
  (1+K)e^{j-K},&j\ge K.
 \end{cases}$$ Its envelope and first-moment constants are independent of $K$, and its exponential tail makes the bootstrap ratio finite. Apply [thm:critical-bootstrap](#thm:critical-bootstrap) at $K$. Since $N_K(K)=1+K$, all three assertions follow. Fixed tile versions follow by applying the same row estimates on their fixed ranges of depth ratios. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-critical-lem-growth-charge"></a>
<div id="critical:lem:growth-charge" class="lemma">

**Lemma 56**. *Assume that no sequence in [def:prohibited-sequence](#def:prohibited-sequence) exists, and fix $0<\alpha<1/2$. Set $$G_f(j)=\log\max_x|f(x+\mathrm i(H-e^{-j}))|.$$ There are constants $C,c>0$ and a sufficiently large $K_0$ such that every $\kappa\ge K_0$ with $\mu_f(\kappa)\ge\kappa^\alpha$ satisfies <a id="critical:eq:growth-charge"></a>$$\label{critical:eq:growth-charge}
 G_f(\kappa+C\log\kappa)-G_f(\kappa-C\log\kappa)
 \ge c\mu_f(\kappa).$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-critical-lem-growth-charge"><summary>Proof of stmt-critical-lem-growth-charge</summary>

<a id="critical:eq:failed-charge"></a>
*Proof.* The function $G_f$ is nondecreasing: apply the maximum principle between two opposite rows and use real symmetry. Suppose the claimed constants do not exist. We may choose $\kappa_n\to\infty$ and $C_n\to\infty$, with $C_n\log\kappa_n=o(\kappa_n)$, such that $b_n:=\mu_f(\kappa_n)\ge\kappa_n^\alpha$ and $$\label{critical:eq:failed-charge}
 G_f(\kappa_n+C_n\log\kappa_n)
       -G_f(\kappa_n-C_n\log\kappa_n)=o(b_n).$$ For clarity one can first set $C_n=n$, require the increment to be less than $b_n/n$, and then choose the violating level larger than any prescribed threshold.

Maximize $\mu(j)e^{-\varepsilon_n|j-\kappa_n|}$, where $\varepsilon_n\downarrow0$ sufficiently slowly, and denote the maximizer by $k_n$, with $B_n=\mu(k_n)\ge b_n$. The maximizing argument in <a href="#critical:eq:discount-normality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:discount-normality">[critical:eq:discount-normality]</a> gives primary normality. The polynomial bound $\mu(j)\le C(1+j)$ shows that $$|k_n-\kappa_n|=O(\varepsilon_n^{-1}\log\kappa_n).$$ Indeed, on the future side use $(1+j)/(1+\kappa_n)\le e^{(j-\kappa_n)/(1+\kappa_n)}$ and choose $\varepsilon_n\ge2/(1+\kappa_n)$; the past side is immediate. We can therefore arrange $$|k_n-\kappa_n|=o(C_n\log\kappa_n),\qquad
 \log\kappa_n+|k_n-\kappa_n|\ll s_n
       \ll C_n\log\kappa_n.$$ Here both ratios denoted by $\ll$ tend to zero. For example, after a further slow choice of $C_n$, one may use $\varepsilon_n=C_n^{-1/3}$ and $s_n=C_n^{2/3}\log\kappa_n$. Set $k_{a,n}=k_n-s_n$; then $k_{a,n}\to\infty$. Choose a horizontal maximizer $x_{a,n}$ of $|f|$ on the ancestor row, take $\omega_n$ to be its point mass, and put $\nu_n=K_{d_{a,n}}*\omega_n$.

For every fixed $\beta>0$, the coarse and anchor hypotheses follow directly from <a href="#critical:eq:polynomial-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:polynomial-bounds">[critical:eq:polynomial-bounds]</a>. Indeed all required coarser tile suprema are $O_A((1+k_n)^2)$, whereas $B_n e^{\beta(k_n-j)}$ is at least $\kappa_n^\alpha e^{\beta(s_n-3)}$ for $j\le k_{a,n}+3$. The latter dominates every fixed polynomial in $\kappa_n$, since $s_n/\log\kappa_n\to\infty$. Similarly the normalized ancestor bound for $P$ is $O((1+k_{a,n})^4)$, and is dominated by $B_n^2e^{2\beta s_n}$. These are supremum estimates, so no bound on the density of the point mass is needed.

Fix a compact target set $\mathcal K\subset\{\Im S<0\}$, and choose a fixed $C'>0$ so that the row $k_n+C'$ is above all the target disks and their fixed enlargements. On the periodic strip from the real row to that row, put $$U_n(s)=G_f(k_n+C')-\log|f(s)|\ge0.$$ At the chosen ancestor point, monotonicity and <a href="#critical:eq:failed-charge" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:failed-charge">[critical:eq:failed-charge]</a> give <a id="critical:eq:small-ancestor-deficit"></a>$$\label{critical:eq:small-ancestor-deficit}
 U_n(x_{a,n}+\mathrm i(H-d_{a,n}))
   =G_f(k_n+C')-G_f(k_{a,n})=o(b_n)=o(B_n).$$ Both levels in this difference lie inside the interval in <a href="#critical:eq:failed-charge" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:failed-charge">[critical:eq:failed-charge]</a>, for sufficiently large $n$.

For any row in the fixed target range, apply positive superharmonic comparison to $U_n$ from the ancestor, using the real bottom. The upper-boundary harmonic-measure law is comparable to $\nu_n$, because its depth is $o(d_{a,n})$. The bottom contribution is nonnegative. It follows that $$\int U_n(x+\mathrm i(H-d_j))\,\,\mathrm d\nu_n(x)=o(B_n)$$ uniformly over that fixed range of $j-k_n$. The comparison can be justified first for the superharmonic truncations $\min\{U_n,R\}$ and then by monotone convergence. Averaging over the target disks has the same bound: their horizontal shifts are $O(d_n)$, and the density of $\nu_n$ changes by bounded factors under those shifts.

Apply [lem:log-deficit](#lem:log-deficit) on a finite covering of the target compact set by disks with fixed inner margins. It yields $$\int \sup_{S\in\mathcal K}
          d_n|q(x+\mathrm iH+d_nS)|^{1/2}\,\,\mathrm d\nu_n(x)
 \le C+o(B_n).$$ Since $B_n\to\infty$, Markov’s inequality proves <a href="#critical:eq:prohibited-Q" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:prohibited-Q">[critical:eq:prohibited-Q]</a>. Together with the preceding normality and ancestor estimates this constructs a prohibited sequence, the required contradiction. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-thm-angle-budget-reduction"></a>
<div id="thm:angle-budget-reduction" class="theorem">

<a id="critical:eq:angle-budget"></a>
**Theorem 57** (Conditional angle-budget reduction). *If no sequence in [def:prohibited-sequence](#def:prohibited-sequence) exists, then for some $\varepsilon>0$ and $C<\infty$, $$\label{critical:eq:angle-budget}
 \int_{k_0}^K\mu_f(k)^2\,\,\mathrm dk\le C(1+K)^{2-\varepsilon}
 \qquad(K\ge k_0).$$ In particular [thm:sequence-exclusion](#thm:sequence-exclusion) will establish this conclusion and [cor:critical-polynomial-bounds](#cor:critical-polynomial-bounds) in the critical case.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-thm-angle-budget-reduction"><summary>Proof of stmt-thm-angle-budget-reduction</summary>

*Proof.* Fix $0<\alpha<1/2$ and split the sufficiently large levels into the high set $\mathcal A=\{k:\mu_f(k)\ge k^\alpha\}$ and its complement. By [critical:lem:growth-charge](#critical:lem:growth-charge), $$\int_{\mathcal A\cap[K_0,K]}\mu_f(k)\,\,\mathrm dk
 \le C\int_{K_0}^K
       [G_f(k+C\log k)-G_f(k-C\log k)]\,\,\mathrm dk.$$ The polynomial bound gives $G_f(v)\le v+C\log(2+v)$. Since $G_f$ is nondecreasing, its positive Stieltjes measure can be used to evaluate the last integral. Each point of that measure is counted for a set of $k$’s of length at most $2C\log K$. Its total mass over the relevant interval, whose upper endpoint is $K+C\log K$, is $O(K)$. The lower endpoint can be kept fixed by increasing $K_0$. Hence $$\int_{\mathcal A\cap[K_0,K]}\mu_f(k)\,\,\mathrm dk=O(K\log K).$$ Multiplying by the bound from [critical:prop:power-saving](#critical:prop:power-saving) gives $$\int_{\mathcal A\cap[K_0,K]}\mu_f(k)^2\,\,\mathrm dk
 \le C K^{2-\varepsilon_1}\log K.$$ On the complementary set the integral is at most $\int_{K_0}^K k^{2\alpha}\,\,\mathrm dk=O(K^{1+2\alpha})$. Both have a positive power saving from $K^2$; decreasing that power slightly absorbs the logarithm and the initial compact range. This proves <a href="#critical:eq:angle-budget" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="critical:eq:angle-budget">[critical:eq:angle-budget]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:model"></a>
### The critical moment law and its first-field model

We now establish the missing input to the critical estimates: the exclusion of the sequences in [def:prohibited-sequence](#def:prohibited-sequence). The exclusion has two parts. A sufficiently steep part of the moment law produces one of the exponential profiles already ruled out by [thm:exponential-obstruction](#thm:exponential-obstruction). Otherwise, after another change of scale, the first field has a nonzero limit. Its limiting impact equation forces both an upper growth estimate and large values near every boundary location. These two estimates are incompatible with the fact that the quotient of its second derivative by the field is holomorphic.

<a id="stmt-thm-sequence-exclusion"></a>
<div id="thm:sequence-exclusion" class="theorem">

**Theorem 58** (Exclusion of the critical sequence). *There is no sequence satisfying [def:prohibited-sequence](#def:prohibited-sequence).*

</div>

We prove the theorem below. Until that proof is completed, neither the angle budget nor the polynomial bounds conditional on this theorem will be used.

<a id="model:moment-subsection"></a>
#### The limiting moment law

<a id="model:primary-normality"></a>
Suppose, for contradiction, that a prohibited sequence is given. Write its primary level, depth, and normalization as $$k=k_n,\qquad d=d_n=e^{-k_n},\qquad B=B_n=\mu(k_n)\longrightarrow\infty.$$ Thus, for some $\varepsilon_n\to0$, $$\label{model:primary-normality}
 \mu(l)\le B e^{\varepsilon_n|l-k|}
 \qquad(l\ge k_0).$$ Expectation without a subscript in a horizontal moment means normalized Lebesgue measure on one period. At physical depth $dD$, set <a id="model:primary-moment"></a>$$\label{model:primary-moment}
 m_n(D)=\frac dB
 \left(\mathbb E\bigl(|f|^2+|q|\bigr)\right)^{1/2}
 =\frac{\mu(k-\log D)}{BD}.$$ Each fixed compact subinterval of $0<D<\infty$ is contained in the domain of this definition for all sufficiently large $n$.

<a id="stmt-model-moment-compactness"></a>
<div id="model:moment-compactness" class="lemma">

<a id="model:moment-properties"></a>
**Lemma 59** (Compactness of the moment law). *After passage to a subsequence, $m_n$ converges locally uniformly on $(0,\infty)$ to a positive function $m$. It satisfies $$\label{model:moment-properties}
 m(1)=1,\qquad m(D)\le D^{-1},\qquad \log m
 \text{ is convex as a function of }D.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-model-moment-compactness"><summary>Proof of stmt-model-moment-compactness</summary>

*Proof.* For a periodic holomorphic function, its horizontal $L^p$ norm, $p\ge1$, is log-convex in the height. One way to see this is to regard horizontal translates of the function as a Banach-space-valued analytic function and apply the three-lines theorem to bounded linear functionals. Equivalently, apply the scalar three-lines theorem followed by the dual description of the $L^p$ norm. We use this for the $L^2$ norm of $f$ and the $L^1$ norm of $q$. If $A$ and $C$ are nonnegative log-convex functions, then their sum is log-convex: the required interpolation inequality follows from Holder’s inequality applied to $A_0^{1-\theta}A_1^\theta+C_0^{1-\theta}C_1^\theta$. Consequently $\log m_n$ is convex. A field which is identically zero can simply be omitted from this argument.

The normalization gives $m_n(1)=1$, and <a href="#model:primary-normality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:primary-normality">[model:primary-normality]</a> gives $$m_n(D)\le D^{-1}\exp(\varepsilon_n|\log D|).$$ Thus $\log m_n$ is uniformly bounded above on every compact subinterval. Convexity and its value zero at $1$ give a lower bound there as well. For example, if $D<1<D_+$, use the convexity inequality at $1$, viewed as a convex combination of $D$ and $D_+$, and the upper bound at $D_+$. For $D>1$, use a point $D_-<1$. Bounds on a slightly larger compact interval bound the slopes of a convex function on the smaller one. Arzela–Ascoli and a diagonal subsequence therefore give a finite locally uniform limit for $\log m_n$. Exponentiating proves positivity, and all the properties in <a href="#model:moment-properties" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:moment-properties">[model:moment-properties]</a> pass to the limit. ◻

</details>

<a id="model:slope-inequality"></a>
Put <a id="model:rho-definition"></a>$$\label{model:rho-definition}
 \rho(x)=-\log m(e^x).$$ This use of $\rho$ concerns only the moment law. It is unrelated to the curvature radius of the original billiard. The function $\rho$ is increasing and locally Lipschitz, and $$\rho(0)=0,\qquad \rho(x)\ge x.$$ Indeed, the convex function $\log m(D)$ tends to $-\infty$ as $D\to\infty$, so each of its one-sided derivatives is strictly negative. With the left derivative used at exceptional points, let $p(x)=\rho'_-(x)>0$. Monotonicity of the one-sided derivative of $\log m$ gives $$\label{model:slope-inequality}
 p(v)\le e^{v-u}p(u)\qquad(v\ge u).$$

<a id="stmt-lem-contact-dichotomy"></a>
<div id="lem:contact-dichotomy" class="lemma">

<a id="model:contact-envelope"></a>
**Lemma 60** (Contact dichotomy). *Fix $c\in(1/2,1)$, and define $$\label{model:contact-envelope}
 \rho_c(x)=cx+\inf_{v\ge x}\bigl(\rho(v)-cv\bigr).$$ A point is called a contact if $\rho(x)=\rho_c(x)$. Exactly one of the following alternatives is needed.*

<a id="model:exponential-moment-tangent"></a>
<a id="model:contact-power-tail"></a>
1.  *There are contacts tending to $+\infty$ at which $p$ is unbounded. In that case there exist $x_j\to\infty$, $P_j=p(x_j)\to
    \infty$, and $D_j=e^{x_j}$ such that $$\label{model:exponential-moment-tangent}
     \frac{m(D_j(1-u/P_j))}{m(D_j)}\longrightarrow e^u$$ uniformly on bounded real $u$-intervals. For every fixed $\alpha_0\in(1/2,c)$, these choices can also satisfy $$\label{model:contact-power-tail}
     \frac{m(D_j(1+v/P_j))}{m(D_j)}
     \le C(1+v)^{-\alpha_0}\qquad(v\ge1),$$ with $C$ independent of $j$.*

<a id="model:rho-two-ended-slope"></a>
<a id="model:rho-coarse-envelope"></a>
<a id="model:rho-fine-envelope"></a>
2.  *The slopes at all sufficiently large contacts are bounded. There exist $x_j\to\infty$, a locally Lipschitz function $\rho_*$ with $\rho_*(0)=0$, and a finite $\lambda\ge1$ such that <a id="model:rho-translate-limit"></a>$$\label{model:rho-translate-limit}
     \rho(x_j+u)-\rho(x_j)\longrightarrow\rho_*(u)$$ locally uniformly, and $$\label{model:rho-two-ended-slope}
     \rho_*(u)=\lambda u+o(|u|)\qquad(u\to+\infty\text{ or }u\to-\infty).$$ There are constants $C,P'>0$, independent of $j$, for which $$\begin{aligned}
    \label{model:rho-coarse-envelope}
     \rho(v)&\ge \rho(x_j)+c(v-x_j)-C&& (v\ge x_j),\\
    \label{model:rho-fine-envelope}
     \rho(v)&\ge \rho(x_j)-P'(x_j-v)-C&& (v\le x_j).
    \end{aligned}$$ Moreover $\rho(x_j)=O(1+x_j)$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-contact-dichotomy"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-contact-dichotomy</summary>

*Proof.* Since $\rho(v)-cv\ge(1-c)v$, the infimum in <a href="#model:contact-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:contact-envelope">[model:contact-envelope]</a> is attained. The same inequality gives $$x\le\rho_c(x)\le\rho(x).$$ The running infimum is locally Lipschitz: when its lower endpoint is moved, its value can increase only because a minimizer lay in the swept interval, where the local Lipschitz bound for $\rho-cx$ applies. On an open interval containing no contact the minimizer remains to the right, so $\rho_c$ is affine of slope $c$. Everywhere, $\rho_c(v)-\rho_c(u)\ge c(v-u)$ for $v\ge u$.

First suppose there are contacts $z_j\to\infty$ with $p(z_j)\to\infty$. By <a href="#model:slope-inequality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:slope-inequality">[model:slope-inequality]</a>, $$p(x)\ge e^{-1}p(z_j)\qquad(z_j-1\le x\le z_j).$$ For large $j$, $\rho(x)-cx$ is strictly increasing on this interval. Each point in it is itself a contact: values between that point and $z_j$ are larger, and values beyond $z_j$ are at least the value at $z_j$ because $z_j$ is a contact.

Set $g=p^{-1/2}$ on this interval. Inequality <a href="#model:slope-inequality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:slope-inequality">[model:slope-inequality]</a> says that $e^{x/2}g(x)$ is nondecreasing. If $\sigma_j$ is the supremum of $g$ on the interval, then $\sigma_j\to0$, and the total variation of $g$ there is $O(\sigma_j)$. To choose a point where this small total variation is locally well distributed, let $\nu_j$ be its variation measure. The elementary weak maximal inequality for intervals gives $$\left|\left\{x:
 \sup_{h>0}\frac{\nu_j((x-h,x+h))}{2h}>
 \sqrt{\sigma_j}\right\}\right|=O(\sqrt{\sigma_j}).$$ Here intervals are restricted to the original unit interval. This inequality follows by selecting disjoint bad intervals and covering their union by their fivefold enlargements. Choose $x_j$ outside this bad set in the middle third of the unit interval. Then, whenever $|h|$ is smaller than its distance to the endpoints, $$|g(x_j+h)-g(x_j)|\le
 2\sqrt{\sigma_j}|h|.$$ Taking $|h|\le g(x_j)=P_j^{-1/2}$ shows that $$\frac{p(x_j+h)}{P_j}\longrightarrow1
 \quad\hbox{uniformly for }|h|\le P_j^{-1/2}.$$ Integration, with $\log(1-u/P_j)=-u/P_j+O(P_j^{-2})$, proves <a href="#model:exponential-moment-tangent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:exponential-moment-tangent">[model:exponential-moment-tangent]</a>.

For the tail estimate write $z=\log(1+v/P_j)$. If $0\le z\le P_j^{-1/2}$, integration of the last slope estimate gives $\rho(x_j+z)-\rho(x_j)\ge P_jz/2$, which is at least a fixed positive multiple of $v$ in this range. At $z=P_j^{-1/2}$ the increase is at least a fixed multiple of $\sqrt{P_j}$. This endpoint is still a contact. For larger $z$, the contact inequality adds at least $c(z-P_j^{-1/2})$. Since $$\log(1+v)\le \log P_j+z+O(1)$$ and $\alpha_0<c$, the increase is at least $\alpha_0\log(1+v)-O(1)$, uniformly for all $v\ge1$. Exponentiating proves <a href="#model:contact-power-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:contact-power-tail">[model:contact-power-tail]</a>.

Now suppose that $p$ is bounded on contacts in a tail. Almost everywhere on the contact set the derivatives of $\rho$ and $\rho_c$ agree, since the two locally Lipschitz functions agree there. Off that set the derivative of $\rho_c$ equals $c$. Consequently $\rho_c$ has a uniform Lipschitz constant $K_1$ on some tail. Extend it to the left with a fixed Lipschitz constant. Consider the anchored translates $$u\longmapsto\rho_c(x+u)-\rho_c(x).$$ They lie in a compact space of anchored Lipschitz functions, with the topology of uniform convergence on compact intervals. Average their point masses over $x\in[x_0,x_0+R]$. A weak limit as $R\to\infty$ is invariant under every anchored translation $$(\mathcal T_h q)(u)=q(u+h)-q(h).$$ Indeed translating the averaging interval changes its normalized measure by at most $2|h|/R$.

<a id="model:envelope-ergodic-path"></a>
The mean increment at $1$ of this invariant law is at least $1$. To check this, telescope the integral: $$\frac1R\int_{x_0}^{x_0+R}
       \bigl(\rho_c(x+1)-\rho_c(x)\bigr)\,\,\mathrm dx
 =
 \frac1R\left(
 \int_{x_0+R}^{x_0+R+1}\rho_c-
 \int_{x_0}^{x_0+1}\rho_c\right),$$ and use $\rho_c(x)\ge x$. Birkhoff’s pointwise ergodic theorem (Durrett 2019, Theorem 6.2.1) <a id="pm-cite-25"></a>[[Durrett2019](#ref-Durrett2019)] for the invertible map $\mathcal T_1$, applied in both directions to the bounded unit increments, now provides a path $q_*$ in the support of the law for which $$\label{model:envelope-ergodic-path}
 \frac{q_*(u)}u\longrightarrow\lambda\ge1
 \qquad(u\to+\infty\text{ or }u\to-\infty).$$ The two limits agree because they are the same invariant conditional expectation of the unit increment. Bounded increments between successive integers extend the conclusion to real $u$. Such a path is approximated locally uniformly by translates with centers $x_j\to\infty$: a neighborhood visited only for bounded $x$ has zero mass in every limiting averaged measure.

We next replace $\rho_c$ by $\rho$. To the right of any fixed compact $u$-interval, <a href="#model:envelope-ergodic-path" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:envelope-ergodic-path">[model:envelope-ergodic-path]</a> gives a fixed interval $[v,w]$ on which the increment of $q_*$ exceeds $c(w-v)$. The approximating translates of $\rho_c$ must therefore have a contact in $[x_j+v,x_j+w]$. Monotonicity of $\rho$, together with $\rho\ge\rho_c$, bounds $\rho(x_j+u)-\rho_c(x_j)$ above and below on every compact interval. It also bounds the local slopes of $\rho$: from <a href="#model:slope-inequality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:slope-inequality">[model:slope-inequality]</a>, $$p(x)\le e\int_{x-1}^x p(v)\,\,\mathrm dv
       =e\bigl(\rho(x)-\rho(x-1)\bigr).$$ Thus a subsequence of the anchored translates of $\rho$ has a locally uniform limit $\rho_*$, and $\rho(x_j)-\rho_c(x_j)=O(1)$.

For completeness, this limit has the same two-ended slope as $q_*$. Fix a small $\eta>0$. For every sufficiently large $|u|$, the increment of $q_*$ on $[u,u+\eta|u|]$ exceeds $c\eta|u|$, by <a href="#model:envelope-ergodic-path" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:envelope-ergodic-path">[model:envelope-ergodic-path]</a> and $\lambda>c$. The same contact argument, followed by passage to the limit, bounds the excess of $\rho_*(u)$ over $q_*(u)$, up to a fixed additive constant, by $K_1\eta|u|$. The lower bound $\rho\ge\rho_c$ bounds the deficit by a fixed constant. Letting $\eta\downarrow0$ proves <a href="#model:rho-two-ended-slope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:rho-two-ended-slope">[model:rho-two-ended-slope]</a>.

Finally, the lower increment bound for $\rho_c$, its uniform Lipschitz bound, and the bounded difference at $x_j$ give <a href="#model:rho-coarse-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:rho-coarse-envelope">[model:rho-coarse-envelope]</a> and <a href="#model:rho-fine-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:rho-fine-envelope">[model:rho-fine-envelope]</a> as long as $v$ remains in the tail. For the remaining left range, use $\rho(v)\ge v$, increasing $P'>\max(K_1,1)$ and the additive constant if necessary. The same Lipschitz bound gives $\rho(x_j)=O(1+x_j)$. ◻

</details>

<a id="model:steep-subsection"></a>
#### The steep-contact alternative

<a id="stmt-model-steep-excluded"></a>
<div id="model:steep-excluded" class="lemma">

**Lemma 61**. *Alternative <span class="upright">(i)</span> of [lem:contact-dichotomy](#lem:contact-dichotomy) is impossible for the moment law of a prohibited sequence.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-model-steep-excluded"><summary>Proof of stmt-model-steep-excluded</summary>

*Proof.* For each fixed $j$, take the original index $n$ sufficiently large and set <a id="model:contact-physical-scales"></a>$$\label{model:contact-physical-scales}
 h_n=H-dD_j,\qquad
 \ell_n=\frac{dD_j}{P_j},\qquad
 m_0=\frac Bd\,m_n(D_j).$$ The diagonal can be chosen so that $$h_n\to H,\qquad \ell_n\to0,\qquad
 m_0\ell_n\to\infty.$$ For the last assertion, first keep $j$ fixed: $m_0\ell_n=B D_jm_n(D_j)/P_j\to\infty$. The distance from $h_n$ to the upper shape wall, in units of $\ell_n$, is $P_j\to\infty$; the lower wall also escapes in these units.

Both <a href="#model:exponential-moment-tangent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:exponential-moment-tangent">[model:exponential-moment-tangent]</a> and <a href="#model:contact-power-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:contact-power-tail">[model:contact-power-tail]</a> can be transferred to the actual moments on the required ranges. Here is the tail detail. Fix $\alpha_0\in(1/2,c)$, and require $\varepsilon_n<(1-\alpha_0)/2$. For each fixed $j$, choose a finite cutoff $D_{\rm cut}$ large enough that the primary bound $m_n(D)\le D^{-1+\varepsilon_n}$ is below a fixed multiple of the right side of <a href="#model:contact-power-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:contact-power-tail">[model:contact-power-tail]</a>, with the normalizing factor $m_n(D_j)$, whenever $D\ge D_{\rm cut}$. Such a cutoff exists because $1-\varepsilon_n>\alpha_0$ and $m_n(D_j)\to m(D_j)>0$. On the finite interval below the cutoff use locally uniform moment convergence. Choose the fixed physical cutoff $0<\delta_b<H/2$ small enough that the enlarged depth range used for submean disks has logarithmic level at least $k_0$. Thus all the coarser depths up to $\delta_b$ are controlled, with a constant independent of $j$.

<a id="model:biased-cancellation"></a>
On the row of height $h_n$, define $$H_x=\frac{|f(x+\mathrm ih_n)|^2+|q(x+\mathrm ih_n)|}{m_0^2}.$$ Its horizontal mean is $1$. Sample $x$ with probability density $H_x$ relative to normalized horizontal measure, and set $m_x=m_0\sqrt{H_x}$; the zero-density set $H_x=0$ can be discarded. In the coordinate $$S=\frac{s-x-\mathrm ih_n}{\ell_n},$$ let $$\mathcal F_x(S)=\frac{f(s)}{m_x},\qquad
 \mathcal Q_x(S)=\frac{q(s)}{m_x^2}.$$ There is an exact cancellation in the expectation: $$\label{model:biased-cancellation}
 \mathbb E_H\bigl(|\mathcal F_x(S)|^2+|\mathcal Q_x(S)|\bigr)
 =
 \frac{\mathbb E\bigl(|f|^2+|q|\bigr)
       \text{ on the row }h_n+\ell_n\Im S}{m_0^2}.$$ The denominator $H_x$ cancels against the sampling density, and the remaining integral is invariant under the horizontal translation $x\mapsto x+\ell_n\Re S$. The transferred local moment law therefore makes <a href="#model:biased-cancellation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:biased-cancellation">[model:biased-cancellation]</a> converge locally uniformly to $e^{2\Im S}$.

<a id="model:sampled-coarse-bound"></a>
Submean estimates applied before taking expectation give the same bounds for suprema on smaller tiles. In a cone of fixed aperture $L$, a dyadic band with depth $D\ge1$ requires only a number of depth-sized tiles depending on $L$. The expected squared size of the fields on this band is at most $C_LD^{-2\alpha_0}$. Choose one $\alpha\in(1/2,\alpha_0)$, independently of $L$. Summation of $D^{2\alpha}C_LD^{-2\alpha_0}$ over dyadic bands proves tightness of the random constants in the pointwise bounds $$\label{model:sampled-coarse-bound}
 \max(|\mathcal F_x(S)|,\sqrt{|\mathcal Q_x(S)|})
 \le C_L(-\Im S)^{-\alpha}$$ for $1\le-\Im S\le\delta_b/\ell_n$ and $|\Re S|\le L(-\Im S)$. Also $$\mathbb P_H(H_x\le a)=\mathbb E\bigl(H_x\mathbf 1_{\{H_x\le a\}}\bigr)\le a.$$ Since $m_0\ell_n\to\infty$, it follows that $m_x\ell_n\to\infty$ in probability.

Now consider the nonnegative subharmonic function $$U_x(S)=|e^{\mathrm iS}\mathcal F_x(S)|^2
       +|e^{2\mathrm iS}\mathcal Q_x(S)|.$$ Its mean tends locally uniformly to $1$. If a nonnegative smooth cutoff equals $1$ on a fixed compact set, integration against its Laplacian shows that the expected Riesz mass of $U_x$ on that set tends to zero: the limiting integral of the Laplacian of the cutoff is zero. The mass itself is nonnegative, so it tends to zero in probability.

We may therefore select deterministic centers and a subsequence with all the following properties: local analytic bounds on an exhaustion of the plane; the bounds <a href="#model:sampled-coarse-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:sampled-coarse-bound">[model:sampled-coarse-bound]</a> for every fixed aperture; $m_x\ell_n\to\infty$; and vanishing Riesz mass on every fixed compact set. To make the quantifier explicit, assign summable failure probabilities to countably increasing apertures and compact sets, choose their bound constants once, and then take the sequence index sufficiently large for the remaining probability conditions. The union of the bad events has probability less than one. This gives fixed eventual constants for each aperture, not constants growing with the sequence index.

The resulting entire limits $(\mathcal F,\mathcal Q)$ obey $$|e^{\mathrm iS}\mathcal F(S)|^2
       +|e^{2\mathrm iS}\mathcal Q(S)|
 \quad\hbox{harmonic}.$$ Each summand is subharmonic, so each is harmonic. An analytic function with harmonic squared modulus is constant. An analytic function with harmonic modulus is also constant: away from its zeros its Laplacian is $|G'|^2/|G|$, and the assertion follows by analytic continuation. Thus $$\mathcal F(S)=c_1e^{-\mathrm iS},\qquad
 \mathcal Q(S)=c_2e^{-2\mathrm iS}.$$ At $S=0$ the normalized sum is exactly $1$, so the limit is nonzero. Moreover $$\mathcal F_x''=(m_x\ell_n)^2\mathcal Q_x\mathcal F_x.$$ Compact convergence and $m_x\ell_n\to\infty$ imply $\mathcal Q\mathcal F=0$. The limit is consequently one of the two nonzero pure exponential profiles in [thm:exponential-obstruction](#thm:exponential-obstruction). All its finite-wall hypotheses were checked above, including a single exponent $\alpha>1/2$ for every fixed aperture. That theorem gives the contradiction. ◻

</details>

<a id="model:selection-subsection"></a>
#### Re-centering and selecting a nonzero first field

We are therefore in alternative <span class="upright">(ii)</span> of [lem:contact-dichotomy](#lem:contact-dichotomy). Choose its $x_j,\rho_*,\lambda$.

<a id="stmt-model-selected-fields"></a>
<div id="model:selected-fields" class="lemma">

<a id="model:star-moment"></a>
<a id="model:new-global-envelope"></a>
<a id="model:selected-cones"></a>
**Lemma 62** (The second scale). *There are depths $d'\to0$, levels $K=-\log d'\to\infty$, normalizations $B'=\mu(K)\to\infty$, and horizontal centers $\xi_n$ with the following properties. Set <a id="model:selected-normalization"></a>$$\label{model:selected-normalization}
 F_n(S)=\frac{d'}{B'}f(\xi_n+\mathrm iH+d'S),\qquad
 Q_n(S)=\left(\frac{d'}{B'}\right)^2q(\xi_n+\mathrm iH+d'S).$$ Then $F_n\to F\not\equiv0$ and $Q_n\to0$ locally uniformly on $\mathbb H_-=\{S:\Im S<0\}$, and $F''/F$ is holomorphic there. The global normalized moment laws converge locally uniformly to $$\label{model:star-moment}
 m_*(D)=\exp\bigl(-\rho_*(\log D)\bigr),\qquad
 \log m_*(D)=-\lambda\log D+o(|\log D|)$$ at both ends of $0<D<\infty$. For fixed $1-c<\beta<1/2$ and some fixed $a>0$, $$\label{model:new-global-envelope}
 \mu(l)\le C B'
 \exp\bigl(\beta(K-l)_++a(l-K)_+\bigr)
 \qquad(l\ge k_0),$$ with $C$ independent of the sequence index. Finally, one can fix $\alpha\in(1/2,1-\beta)$ so that, for every fixed aperture $A$, $$\label{model:selected-cones}
 \max(|F_n(S)|,\sqrt{|Q_n(S)|})
 \le C_A(-\Im S)^{-\alpha}$$ when $1\le-\Im S\le\delta_b/d'$ and $|\Re S|\le A(-\Im S)$, eventually for that aperture.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-model-selected-fields"><summary>Proof of stmt-model-selected-fields</summary>

*Proof.* For each fixed $j$, take the original index $n$ sufficiently large and put $$d'=d e^{x_j},\qquad K=k-x_j,\qquad B'=\mu(K).$$ The identity $$\frac{B'}B=e^{x_j}m_n(e^{x_j})$$ shows that $K,B'\to\infty$ are compatible with this order of choices. We also impose $s_n>x_j+3$, so the ancestor cutoff lies strictly below the new target level. The new normalized moment law is $$\frac{m_n(e^{x_j}D)}{m_n(e^{x_j})},$$ which tends, after the diagonal selection, to <a href="#model:star-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:star-moment">[model:star-moment]</a>.

<a id="model:moment-ratio-change"></a>
We spell out the global envelope because its constants must remain uniform after diagonalization. With $v=k-l$, $$\label{model:moment-ratio-change}
 \frac{\mu(l)}{B'}=
 e^{v-x_j}\frac{m_n(e^v)}{m_n(e^{x_j})}.$$ On a finite $v$-range, the limiting estimates <a href="#model:rho-coarse-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:rho-coarse-envelope">[model:rho-coarse-envelope]</a> and <a href="#model:rho-fine-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:rho-fine-envelope">[model:rho-fine-envelope]</a> imply an upper exponent $1-c$ for $v\ge x_j$ and $P'-1$ for $v\le x_j$. Choose $\beta>1-c$ and $a>\max(P'-1,0)$. Since $\rho(x_j)=O(1+x_j)$, primary normality bounds the logarithm of <a href="#model:moment-ratio-change" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:moment-ratio-change">[model:moment-ratio-change]</a> by $$C(1+x_j)+\varepsilon_n|v|.$$ If $\varepsilon_n$ is small compared with $\beta$ and $a$, this is absorbed by the chosen envelope for $|v|\ge C_0(1+x_j)$, with $C_0$ fixed sufficiently large. On the remaining finite interval take $n$ large enough for moment convergence with a fixed multiplicative error. This proves <a href="#model:new-global-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:new-global-envelope">[model:new-global-envelope]</a> with one constant $C$.

Let $k_a=k-s_n$ and $\omega,\nu$ be the ancestors and measures in [def:prohibited-sequence](#def:prohibited-sequence). To apply [prop:weighted-bootstrap](#prop:weighted-bootstrap), take an old coarse exponent $0<\beta_0<\beta$. For $l\le k_a+3$, the ratio of the new coarse normalization to the old one equals <a id="model:ancestor-domination"></a>$$\label{model:ancestor-domination}
 \frac{B'e^{\beta(K-l)}}{Be^{\beta_0(k-l)}}
 =
 \frac{B'}B e^{-\beta x_j}
 e^{(\beta-\beta_0)(k-l)}
 \ge
 \frac{B'}B e^{-\beta x_j}
 e^{(\beta-\beta_0)(s_n-3)}.$$ For fixed $j$, the last expression tends to infinity. We can therefore make it at least one before proceeding to the next $j$. The same comparison, squared, applies to the absolute ancestor integral of $P$. Thus the coarse hypotheses of the weighted bootstrap hold with constants independent of $j$. The global envelope already has this uniformity, so the resulting weighted $L^2$ bounds do as well.

For each fixed $j$, the new $q$-field on a fixed compact set is the primary $q$-field on another fixed compact set, multiplied by the finite factor $m_n(e^{x_j})^{-2}$. The primary convergence to zero in $\nu$-probability can therefore be imposed to any prescribed tolerance before advancing $j$. Hence the new $q$-field tends to zero in probability on compact sets.

Weighted submean estimates now give tightness of the analytic fields on every compact subset of $\mathbb H_-$. They also give pointwise cone tightness. At depth ratio $D\ge1$, the coarse part of <a href="#model:new-global-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:new-global-envelope">[model:new-global-envelope]</a> bounds the weighted field norm by $CD^{-(1-\beta)}$. Summing depth-sized tile suprema over dyadic bands, with any fixed $\alpha\in(1/2,1-\beta)$, proves tightness of the constants in <a href="#model:selected-cones" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="model:selected-cones">[model:selected-cones]</a>. Fine tiles use the bounded change of the density of $\nu$ on shifts of order the ancestor depth. For tiles coarser than that depth, the necessary tile estimates are precisely the explicit coarse hypotheses of the weighted bootstrap. Thus no translation invariance of $\nu$ is required.

Choose deterministic centers on events with these compact and cone bounds and with the $q$-field small, using summable exceptional probabilities as in the preceding proof. Extract a locally uniform limit $(F,0)$. If $F$ were zero, its compact smallness and the coarser bound with exponent $\alpha>1/2$ would violate [thm:no-trivial-profile](#thm:no-trivial-profile); the global normalization at the target is $B'=\mu(K)$, as that theorem requires. Therefore $F\not\equiv0$.

Each quotient $F_n''/F_n=(d')^2q$ is holomorphic. Around any zero of $F$, choose a small circle containing no other zero and no zero on the circle.
